nodes.name: Ops Endpoint
nodes.notes:
POST { "window_hours": 24 } - the window is a parameter so the edge-case runner
can ask about the last few minutes rather than the last day.

nodes.name: Read Audit
nodes.notes:
Only the window is read, not the whole log. The audit table is the fastest-growing
thing in the system - several rows per lead - so a report that reads all of it gets
slower every day it runs.

nodes.name: Public Metrics
nodes.notes:
Also keeps the Respond node off the fan-out. n8n's validator infers roles from node
TYPE as well as name, and reads a respondToWebhook sitting directly among sibling
branches as an error handler wired to the wrong output - so the two nodes that
genuinely belong on separate branches are the email renderer and this one.

nodes.name: Respond Metrics
nodes.notes:
Reached only on the webhook path. A Respond node in an execution that started from
a schedule trigger has nothing to answer and is simply skipped, which is why both
entry points can share one computation.

nodes.name: Send Report
nodes.notes:
Sent every day, including quiet ones. This is the exception to the "stay silent
when there is nothing to say" rule that the rest of the system follows, and the
reason is that this mail doubles as the heartbeat: its ABSENCE is the signal that
the instance is down. A digest that only arrives when something is wrong cannot
tell you it stopped arriving.

parameters.content:
## LP-07 Ops Report

Daily 08:00 email **and** `POST /webhook/lp-ops {"window_hours":1}` returning the same figures as JSON. One computation, two renderings - the number in the inbox and the number on a dashboard cannot disagree.

**Leads with problems, not volume.** "47 leads processed" gets skimmed; "3 dead letters, 2 SLA breaches, 1 lead with no owner" gets read. Dead letters are listed **by id**, because a count is a number and an id is work you can do.

**Sent even on quiet days**, deliberately - unlike every other notification here. It is the heartbeat: a digest that only arrives when something is wrong can never tell you it stopped arriving.
